candidate.answerReason: Every integer strictly between the endpoints has a proper divisor supplied by one of the factors of n!.

methods.label: Find a divisor of every candidate
methods.explanation:
For \(n=2\), the interval is strictly between \(3\) and \(4\), so it contains no integers.

Now suppose \(n\ge3\). Every integer strictly between \(n!+1\) and \(n!+n\) has the form
\[
n!+k,\qquad 2\le k\le n-1.
\]
The useful observation is that \(k\) is one of the factors in \(n!=1\cdot2\cdots n\). Therefore \(n!/k\) is a positive integer, and
\[
n!+k=k\left(\frac{n!}{k}+1\right).
\]
Here \(k\ge2\), and the other factor is also at least \(2\). Thus every candidate is composite. This covers every integer in the open interval, so there are \(\boxed{0}\) primes, choice \(\boxed{\text{A}}\).
methods.levelReason: The proof uses the supplied factorial definition and the elementary characterization of composite numbers by a nontrivial factorization.

candidate.annotationRationale: The target is proving that every candidate is composite. Factors and factorial notation explain why each candidate has a divisor greater than one. Prime valuations and congruence machinery are unnecessary.

review.mathematicalCheck: For n=2 the interval contains no integers. Otherwise every candidate is n!+k with 2≤k≤n−1, and equals k(n!/k+1), a product of two integers at least 2. Thus every candidate is composite.
